A.summary: Trémais tells the minister that M. Bigot, however reprehensible for his 'commerce immense' and the abuses that followed, cannot justly be accused of having alone caused Canada's ills and the prodigious rise of its expenses: in the posts the military is 'absolument despote' over works, stores, provisions and rations; governor and intendant were 'fantômes' governed by Péan, Mercier and their secretaries, backed by a man raised from butcher's boy (the munitionnaire by the sense); a portrait, apparently of Montcalm, ends 'personne n'a plus contribué que lui'.
A.en:
Although I have reason to expect that you will have received the letter I had the honour to write to you by M. de Joannes,
aide-major of the Languedoc regiment, I have nevertheless thought it my duty to take the liberty of sending you a copy herewith.
Everything in it, My Lord, shows the haste with which I was obliged to write it; but on comparing it since with what my
instruction prescribes, it seemed to me that, being unable for the present to procure you clarifications such as you
desire them, I had nothing to change in the general account it contains. I shall only add that whatever difficulties I may
meet [in?] my inquiries, I shall nevertheless push them as far as my feeble lights can lead them, and I dare assure you
that I shall omit none of the means that decency will allow me to use to bring the abuses to light.

B.summary: Trémais reports that the papers were sent to Trois-Rivières before he could use them and that he has only general talk to go on: Bigot's fortune made by trade, the troops' insatiable claims, Montcalm's demands, real but enormous consumption, no rolls, the soldier left to plunder. The text is the ministry's own decipherment, transcribed here; it supplied the key.
B.en:
I had the honour to inform you, a week after my arrival at Quebec, that M. Bigot had put me in charge of the office of funds,
of that of the troops and of the detail of the stores; but I had hardly taken up my duties when the arrival of the enemy in the
river made it necessary to send to Trois-Rivières all the papers concerning the service, and I found myself deprived of
everything that could give me some instruction on the branches entrusted to me. The other means of obtaining legal proofs
failed me equally. I shall even admit to you, My Lord, that I do not foresee that, whatever inquiries I may make, I shall manage
to procure you any. Fraudulent business is ordinarily done without writing; and it is natural to believe that if there had been
any here, the people who hold it would not be at all disposed to show it. I therefore see myself obliged to stop at general
talk:
